title: South Asia LNG demand growth derailed as Middle East conflict exposes critical supply vulnerabilities
gist: Wood Mackenzie says the Strait of Hormuz closure cut Qatari and UAE LNG to South Asia, flipping 2026 regional LNG demand from a projected +2.7 Mt (+7%) to a decline of about 6 Mt. Countries with concentrated supply (Pakistan, Bangladesh) were hit hardest, while India's diversification and tiered demand management cushioned the shock; emergency measures only postpone fiscal costs.

themes.theme: Hormuz closure and South Asia LNG demand reversal

insights.claim: South Asian LNG demand, previously projected to grow 2.7 Mt (7%) in 2026, is now expected to fall by around 6 Mt after the Strait of Hormuz closure cut off Qatari and UAE LNG, and the post-2026 outlook has been materially downgraded.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A swing of roughly 8.7 Mt versus the prior forecast removes a key marginal growth buyer from the global LNG market; watch spot pricing and the pace of new supply contracting.
insights.quote: LNG demand across South Asia, which had been projected to grow by 2.7 million tonnes (Mt), or 7%, in 2026, is now expected to decline by around 6 Mt
insights.locator: South Asian LNG markets have absorbed one of the most severe supply shocks

insights.claim: Nearly 90% of Qatari and UAE LNG shipped through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025 was destined for Asia, making Asia the region most exposed to the closure.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Asian importers carry the concentrated chokepoint risk, so Hormuz disruption is primarily an Asian demand and price story.
insights.quote: In 2025, nearly 90% of Qatari and UAE LNG shipments through the Strait were destined for Asia, making the region the most affected.
insights.locator: In 2025, nearly 90% of Qatari and UAE

insights.claim: The spike in spot prices relative to contracted LNG prices caused fiscal crises and cut gas demand by over 3 Mt in Bangladesh and about 1.5 Mt each in India and Pakistan.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Price-driven demand destruction quantifies how much South Asian demand is elastic to spot spikes, which helps size downside in importer-linked volumes.
insights.locator: The resulting spike in spot prices

themes.theme: Pakistan: single-source dependence and take-or-pay burden

insights.claim: Pakistan sourced 99% of its 2025 LNG imports from Qatar, and the Hormuz closure cut Pakistan-bound LNG by up to 0.4 Mt per month from March to November 2026, producing over 2.5 Mt of gas demand destruction.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Pakistan is the clearest case of concentration risk becoming demand loss; it frames how single-supplier importers are repriced.
insights.locator: Pakistan has been the most severely affected market

insights.claim: Pakistan re-entered the spot LNG market in April 2026 after a two-year absence but had limited success at high prices, and it remains liable for daily FSRU take-or-pay charges regardless of whether cargoes arrive.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Fixed infrastructure charges amplify the fiscal drain when cargoes do not arrive, raising credit stress for the importer.
insights.quote: Pakistan remains liable for daily FSRU under take-or-pay charges regardless of cargo arrivals.
insights.locator: The country re-entered the spot LNG market

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie cut its Pakistan LNG demand forecast to 3.7 Mt in 2027 from 6.6 Mt in 2025, expects committed volumes to exceed demand through 2030, and projects uncontracted volumes above 90% by the early 2030s.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Contracted supply exceeding demand points to resale or renegotiation pressure on Pakistan's long-term LNG contracts.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie has reduced its LNG demand forecast for Pakistan

themes.theme: Bangladesh: spot-market exposure and fiscal strain

insights.claim: Bangladesh, unable to raise domestic gas output or draw on diversified supply, was forced into the spot market under the worst conditions, with gas shortages causing prolonged power outages and a greater reliance on coal.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: LNG shortfalls in weak-supply importers shift power generation toward coal, supporting coal demand in the region.
insights.locator: Unable to lift domestic gas production

insights.claim: Petrobangla bought spot cargoes from Gunvor and Vitol for March delivery at US$23-28/mmbtu, and Bangladesh paid an average of over US$18/mmbtu for spot LNG between March and June 2026, pressuring government subsidies.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Spot prices far above contract levels turn LNG imports into a subsidy and balance-of-payments problem, a sovereign credit risk to monitor.
insights.locator: Petrobangla procured spot cargoes from Gunvor and Vitol

themes.theme: India: tiered demand management as a resilience model

insights.claim: India handled the shock better by using tiered demand management that kept city gas distribution unaffected while cutting gas to the fertiliser, refinery and industrial sectors in March and April.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Prioritising residential over industrial users limits social disruption but shifts the pain to industrial output and margins.

insights.claim: India's LNG tender award prices ranged US$16.8-18.8/mmbtu from March to June 2026 and rose to US$26.4/mmbtu by September, yet tendering demand stayed robust throughout.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Robust tendering at US$26+/mmbtu shows India's price tolerance, which helps set the global marginal price for LNG.
insights.quote: India's tender award prices ranged from US$16.8–18.8/mmbtu between March and June 2026, rising to US$26.4/mmbtu by September.

insights.claim: Daily urea production in India rose by 12,000-15,000 tonnes and hit records of 25.19 LMT in May and 25.37 LMT in June, supported by government subsidies, despite the gas curtailments to fertiliser makers.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Subsidy-backed output shows India protected fertiliser supply at fiscal cost, relevant to agri inputs and subsidy budgets.

themes.theme: Policy responses, fiscal limits and long-term lessons

insights.claim: Emergency measures such as gas rationing, power cuts, tariff increases and extra budget allocations only postpone costs rather than resolve them, and if hostilities continue governments will have to choose between energy security and fiscal stability.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The conflict's duration is the key variable for South Asian sovereign and utility credit and for the trajectory of regional LNG demand.
insights.quote: Wood Mackenzie cautions that these responses postpone costs rather than resolve them.
insights.locator: Governments across the region have implemented emergency measures

insights.claim: Countries that had diversified supply sources and used multiple pricing mechanisms came through the crisis in far better shape than those that had not.
insights.speaker: Johnson Quadros, Head of Gas and LNG research at Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Expect importers to favour supplier diversification and flexible pricing, which reshapes demand for contracts from different LNG sellers.
insights.quote: Countries that had diversified their supply sources and established multiple pricing mechanisms came through this crisis in far better shape than those that had not.
insights.locator: The Middle East conflict has exposed the structural vulnerabilities

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects 60% LNG demand growth through 2040 with South and Southeast Asia central to it, and warns that the gap between today's supply crisis and a future risk of oversupply creates uncertainty for buyers and sellers.
insights.speaker: Johnson Quadros, Head of Gas and LNG research at Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The long-run demand case is intact but depends on affordable supply; buyers who skip lessons on diversification and trading capability risk a repeat in a larger market.
insights.quote: The disconnect between today's supply crisis and tomorrow's risk of oversupply creates real uncertainty for both buyers and sellers.
insights.locator: Affordable LNG is essential to drive the 60% demand growth
